planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown shrubs in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; give it room to develop its full arching, fountain-like habit, since unlike the compact 'Crispa' cultivar of S. incisa this species is grown as a full-sized specimen shrub.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Tanaka's stephanandra is a larger, more vigorous Japanese relative of cutleaf stephanandra, forming a substantial mounded, arching shrub with long, gracefully bowing canes. The deeply lobed, coarsely toothed, maple-like leaves are larger than those of S. incisa and turn strong shades of orange, red, and purple in autumn, often the shrub's best ornamental feature. Small clusters of greenish-white star-shaped flowers appear along the branches in early summer but are secondary to the foliage and winter bark display. As the plant matures the thin bark on older canes peels and exfoliates to reveal warm cinnamon-orange inner bark, giving multi-season interest in a shrub border or woodland edge where winter stem color can be appreciated. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes at ground level every few years to keep the arching habit youthful and encourage fresh, colorful bark.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown shrubs in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to part shade; blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to part shade; Manchurian pearl bush is a hardy species native to Korea and northeastern China that produces an upright, multi-stemmed shrub with narrower, finely serrated, elliptic leaves than the more familiar Exochorda racemosa. In mid-spring, short racemes of pure white, five-petaled flowers open from round, pearl-like buds along the previous year's wood, covering the shrub for one to two weeks before dropping cleanly. It is among the most cold-hardy pearlbushes, tolerating harsher winters than the showier hybrid selections, which makes it a useful choice for colder gardens wanting an early white-flowering shrub. Give it an uncrowded position where its slightly informal, twiggy winter silhouette is not the focal point, and thin out a few of the oldest stems at the base every few years to keep flowering wood vigorous.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown shrubs in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Wilson's pearl bush is a robust, large-flowered variety of Exochorda giraldii, collected in western China by E.H. Wilson, that grows into a substantially larger, more vigorous shrub than the typical species. In mid-spring it produces exceptionally large, pure white, crepe-textured flowers up to two inches across, held in loose racemes along arching branches, generally considered among the showiest displays in the genus. New growth emerges with a coppery-bronze tint before maturing to fresh green, adding an extra season of color contrast before bloom. Because of its ultimate size, give it a permanent position at the back of a shrub border or as a specimen where it can develop its full, broad, upright-arching form without crowding. Thin a portion of the oldest wood at ground level right after flowering to renew flowering vigor on a plant of this scale.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; an old, deep-pink-flowered selection of beauty bush that flowers most heavily and colors best in full sun.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; 'Rosea' is a long-cultivated selection of beauty bush chosen for flowers in a noticeably deeper, richer rose-pink than the pale-pink typical species, held in the same dense, yellow-throated, tubular clusters that smother the arching branches for one to two weeks in late spring. It shares the straight species' graceful, fountain-like habit, peeling tan bark, and drought tolerance once established, differing mainly in flower color intensity rather than size or hardiness. Full sun produces the heaviest bloom and deepest color; too much shade or overly rich soil encourages soft, leggy growth at the expense of flowers. After bloom the shrub is a plain but unobtrusive green backdrop, so site it where later-season neighbors can take over visual interest.
